newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Feb 25.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Feb 25.

text.p: Fresh cracks emerged in the government's coalition agreement on Monday over a secret plan to sell six small power stations that goes against NZ First's election policy of opposing further privatisation. The disclosure drew taunts from Labour leader Helen Clark that NZ First had betrayed voters at National's behest. "How many more secret privatisations did NZ First sign up to during its coalition talks?" Clark asked. Page 1.

The government has overpaid MPs through their superannuation fund, in some cases by more than NZ$10,000. It is now retrieving payments -- some paid for more than three years -- by cancelling the government's contribution to the super funds of MPs who were overpaid. Page 1.

NZ First's Maori MPs will hold their first caucus on Tuesday morning to discuss their support for embattled MP Tukoroirangi Morgan when he delivers his maiden speech today. Te Tai Tonga MP Tu Wyllie said he would talk to Morgan at the meeting about the need to show some humility during his maiden speech, scheduled for 5:45pm. Page 2.

ACT NZ will ask Parliament's business committee to discuss the colourful maiden speech of Alliance MP Pam Corkery when it meets today. Corkery's speech last week ignored parliamentary convention by criticising other MPs and used frank and colourful language to do so. ACT's representative on the committee, Ken Shirley, said he would raise the matter at its meeting this afternoon. Page 2.

Political expression has been allowed as a defence against defamation claims by former prime minister David Lange. The High Court at Auckland on Monday refused an application by Lange to have the defence struck out of a defamation case over a North and South magazine column. Lange is suing Auckland University political scientist Joe Atkinson and Australian Consolidated Press NZ over a 1995 column criticising his Beehive performance. Page 2.

Publisher Independent Newspapers has been hit by one-off costs in Australia and the United States in the past six months, but on Monday managed to post a $26.19 million profit, just ahead of the previous corresponding period. The bottom-line profit for the six months to the end of December was marginally better than the $25.96 million in the same period in 1995. Page 14.

INL may give up its plans to buy a substantial shareholding in pay television company Sky, if it can't get the right conditions for the deal, managing director Mike Robson says. Independent Newspapers has been negotiating for more than five months to buy up to 83 percent of Sky and analysts have suggested a price tag valuing all of Sky at between $600 million and $800 million. Page 14.

Brierley Investments' bid to buy Conrad Black's remaining five percent stake in newspaper publisher John Fairfax Holdings was temporarily stalled on Monday with Fairfax shareholders voting against approval of the move. A spokeswoman for the Australian Stock Exchange said Fairfax had confirmed that final counting from Friday's poll had resulted in shareholder's rejection of the bid. Page 14.

Property sales and a special dividend helped Colonial Motor Co to a 17 percent rise in first-half net profit despite a lower trading result, the company said on Monday. Net profit for the six months ended December 31 of $6.17 million was up from $5.27 million for the corresponding period of 1995. Page 14.

Goodwill writedowns after the acquisitions of new businesses had pushed Designer Textiles to a $7.12 million loss in the latest nine-month period to December 31, the company said on Monday. Designer Textiles, which said it was "clearing the decks for the future" after the acquisition from LWR of Auckland Knitting Mills and Synthetic Dyeworks and the purchase of Logan Textiles (Brisbane), wrote off $8.77 million in intangible assets. Page 14.

Diversified investment group Hellaby Holdings has reported a net $6.28 million profit in the six months to December 31. The result, which was on a par with the 1995 period's bottom-line $6.22 million, included the restructured group's first tax payment in many years of $1.5 million. Operating profit before tax and minorities of $8.66 million was 24 percent up on last year's $7 million. Page 14.

Cedenco expects to return to profit this financial year after posting a loss in the year to September of just over $6 million. Chairman Basil Logan told the annual meeting in Gisborne on Monday that the turn in fortune was expected from restructuring of the company that has moved tomato growing and processing to Austalia in a joint venture with Cerebos. Page 14.
